hints: Focus on the gas first, the only common alkaline gas you meet in tests is ammonia, so ask yourself how it is released from ammonium ions.
Remember that $\text{NH}_4^+$ only gives $\text{NH}_3$ when warmed with a base that can remove a proton from it.
Look through the four organic substances and pick out the one that is strongly basic enough to deprotonate $\text{NH}_4^+$, just like $\text{NaOH}$ would.
walkthrough:
**Identify the alkaline gas**

Think like a detective. The alkaline gas that turns damp red litmus blue is almost always ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$.

So the question is really: which substance can liberate $\text{NH}_3$ from $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$?

**Recall how ammonia is released**

Ammonium salts release ammonia when warmed with a base. The base takes $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{NH}_4^+$.

General rule:
$$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{base} \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{conjugate acid}$$

**Test the sodium ethoxide**

$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{ONa}$ contains the ethoxide ion, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$, which is a strong base, similar to $\text{OH}^-$.

It reacts on warming:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^- + \text{NH}_4^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Conclude the answer**

Only the strongly basic alkoxide can do this. Acids, neutral alcohols and esters cannot remove $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{NH}_4^+$ to make $\text{NH}_3$.

options.A: CH3CO2H is ethanoic acid, an acid. It cannot act as a base toward NH4+, so it will not liberate NH3. If anything, adding acid suppresses ammonia formation.
options.B: CH3CH2OH is ethanol, a neutral and very weak acid. It is far too weak a base to deprotonate NH4+, so no NH3 is produced on warming.
options.C: CH3CO2CH3 is methyl ethanoate, a neutral ester. It has no basic hydroxide or alkoxide ion available to react with NH4+, so no alkaline gas forms.
options.D: CH3CH2ONa is sodium ethoxide and provides the strong base CH3CH2O-. On warming it deprotonates NH4+ to give NH3 gas plus ethanol, exactly like NaOH would.
